# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1-24 (Extended v170)

## Setting and Time
Multiple periods spanning French Revolution to 1832, continuing through evening of 24th June 1832 (rioting) and winter Year 6. Primary locations include Paris—Rue Plumet (Valjean's house), Place de la Bastille, Prison Chargemagne, Rue des Filles-du-Calvaire No. 6 (Gillenormand residence), Champ-de-Mars, Halles district, Rue du Pont-aux-Choux, Rue de Thorigny, Marché Saint-Jean, Rue des Billettes, Rue Saint-Denis, Rue de la Chanvrerie, Rue de la Petite-Truanderie, Rue Mondétour, Pointe Saint-Eustache, Rue du Cygne, Rue des Prêcheurs, Rue Blomet, Rue de Rivoli, Place Louis XV, Champs-Élysées, Esplanade, bridge of the Invalides, Hôtel des Princes, Hôtel Meurice, Rue Saint-Honoré, Passage Delorme, Place du Palais-Royal, Rue de Béthisy, Rue des Bourdonnais, Rue de la Poterie, Rue du Contrat-Social, Marché-aux-Poirées. English provincial towns (Ravenmere, Elmhaven, Ostcombe, Wilwick, Salcombe, Dunstead, Staveford, Gulhaven, Kelmere, Kelford, Pontoise, Dungate). **Late night rumor/claim (winter Year 5)**: Yera Stenworth confided fire at Dunstead granary set deliberately—unverified. **Late night rumor/claim (winter Year 5)**: Fenelle Lindmere confided Stenson family once owed blood debt to Stenenridge family—unverified. **Unverified claim (mid-June 1832)**: Marald revealed Stenson family once owed blood debt to Stenenridge family. **New unverified claim (autumn Year 6)**: Stenenridge mill ledger rewritten after flood. **Kassa Brackick and Volan Stenworth married at Staveford with half parish present; couple lived in Staveford thereafter. Later, Kassa Stenson went to Dungate.** **Taric Corrley quit Staveford after quarrel, took lodgings in Dungate. Marald Corrford quit Dunstead after quarrel, took lodgings in Salcombe.** **Fenelle Lindmere followed him to Salcombe within the month.** **Ismira Stenson quit Dungate for good after quarrel and took lodgings in Elmhaven (winter Year 6).** **Matho Stenson went along to live in Elmhaven as well (winter Year 6).**

**Autumn Year 6 provincial observations**: Ferald Stenworth complained of aching back; Thizek Stenenridge and Ferald predicted rain (wrongly); Elra Corrford laughed at story others didn't find funny; Bremira Corrford bought and regretted ribbon at stall. **Elra Corrford swore to Ferald to plant an orchard on slope above Ravenmere, shook on it.** **Elra and Bremira Corrford talked of weather, harvest, lame horse.** **Isvie Stenworth counted coins twice, came up penny short.** **Elra walked long way round to avoid muddy square.** **Luena Stenenridge told by Rozek she looked tired (Rozek did not deny it).** **Rozek Stenenridge fell asleep in chair before fire caught.** **Luena Stenenridge gave jade mirror to Rozek.** **Luena complained of aching back, as usual.** **Winter Year 6 provincial observations**: **Kassa Stenson complained of an aching back, as usual.** **Kassa read the almanac aloud, mispronouncing half the saints.** **Kassa watched clouds and predicted rain, wrongly.** **Kassa counted coins twice and still came up penny short.** **Taric Corrley walked long way round to avoid muddy square.** **Taric laughed at story nobody else found funny.** **Taric Corrley and Kassa Stenson talked of nothing much—weather, harvest, lame horse.** **Kassa Stenson and Taric Corrley discussed: "The price of salt is a scandal."** Frost silvered hedges overnight; bells rang thinly for vespers; wind smelled of salt and tar; bees hummed in lavender; dogs barked briefly; carts laden with turnips creaked past well; light went early.

## Jean Valjean and Cosette (through evening 24th June 1832)
**The wound**: Day following Jondrette visit, Valjean appeared with large inflamed wound on left arm resembling burn. Detained one month with fever; refused doctor. Cosette devoted herself to care. Recovered through March-April.

**Mysterious journeys and nocturnal manuscript**: Valjean took occasional journeys, destination unknown. Found carrying large club in garden dusk. Cosette discovered philosophical manuscript on bench—meditation on love as divine spark, recognized writer as Marius.

**Imminent departure (late June 1832)**: Morning of 24th June, Valjean told Cosette he must settle affairs; she must hold herself in readiness; linen to pack; obliged to go on journey; all to be ready in one week. **Possible destination: England.**

**Thénardier sighting and surveillance**: Caught sight of Thénardier in disguise during spring Year 6. Since that day, seen him repeatedly; certain Thénardier prowling neighborhood. Now rarely goes out with Cosette; spends time meditating on isolated slopes of Champ-de-Mars.

## Marius and Cosette's Romance (through evening 24th June 1832)
**Recognition and revelation**: Upon reading Marius's manuscript, Cosette acknowledged she had never forgotten him, had always loved him. "Fire had been smothered, and had smouldered for a time," but now "it burst forth afresh."

**Garden encounters**: Beginning autumn Year 5, Marius came every evening, entering by forcing old gate. **At height of love's voluptuousness, Marius remained absolutely chaste.** Love described as "chaste, almost shy."

**Confessions of identity (spring Year 6)**: **Cholera decimated Paris during that month.** **Marius told Cosette**: orphan, name Marius Pontmercy, lawyer, lived by writing for publishers, father was colonel and hero, on bad terms with rich grandfather, hinted at being baron. **Cosette told Marius**: brought up at Petit-Picpus convent, mother dead, father's name M. Fauchelevent, very good, gave greatly to poor.

**Marius's response and last arrangement (late June 1832)**: For last six weeks, Marius slowly taken possession of Cosette. **Upon learning of Valjean's plan to take Cosette to England in one week**: Marius declared this gravest atrocity. **Protested he has no money (owes more than ten louis to Courfeyrac), old hat, coat missing buttons, shirt ragged, elbows torn, boots leak.** **Arranged to meet in garden 26th June at nine o'clock at dusk.**

**Marius's despair and departure to barricade (evening 24th June 1832)**: Approached grating to garden. Displaced bar and rushed headlong in. Cosette not at waiting spot. Traversed thicket, approached recess—not there. Raised eyes; shutters closed. Made tour of garden; deserted. Returned to house and knocked repeatedly, called "Cosette!" imperiously. No reply. **Fixed despairing eyes on dismal house, black and silent as tomb. Seated himself on flight of steps, heart filled with sweetness and resolution. Blessed his love, said to himself that since Cosette was gone, all that was left for him was to die.** **A voice summoned him through twilight to barricade of Rue de la Chanvrerie, producing effect of voice of destiny.** **Wished to die; opportunity presented itself; knocked at door of tomb; hand in darkness offered him key.** **Mad with grief, no longer conscious of anything fixed or solid in brain, incapable of accepting anything of fate after two months intoxication of youth and love, overwhelmed by all reveries of despair, had but one desire: to make speedy end of all.** **Thrust aside bar, emerged from garden, said: "I will go."** **Emerged from Rue Plumet by boulevard, traversed Esplanade and bridge of Invalides, Champs-Élysées, Place Louis XV, reached Rue de Rivoli. Shops open, gas burning under arcades, women making purchases, people eating ices and cakes. Few posting-chaises setting out from Hôtel des Princes and Hôtel Meurice.** **Entered Rue Saint-Honoré through Passage Delorme. Shops closed, merchants chatting at doors, windows lighted, cavalry on Place du Palais-Royal.** **Followed Rue Saint-Honoré; fewer lighted windows, shops shut, no one chatting, street growing sombre, crowd increasing. No one speaking in throng, yet dull deep murmur arose.** **Willed with will of man who hopes no more. Found means to traverse throng, pass bivouac of troops, shun patrols, avoid sentinels. Made circuit, reached Rue de Béthisy, directed course towards Halles. At corner of Rue des Bourdonnais, no more lanterns.** **Passed zone of crowd, passed limits of troops; found himself in something startling. No passer-by, no soldier, no light, no one; solitude, silence, night, chill seized him.** **By circuit, reached lane he judged Rue de la Poterie; near middle, came in contact with overturned wagon. Foot recognized pools, gullies, scattered paving-stones. Barricade begun there, abandoned. Climbed over stones.** **Walked near street-posts, guided himself along walls. Beyond barricade, perceived something white: two white horses from omnibus Bossuet harnessed in morning, straying all day, halted there with weary patience.** **Left horses behind. Approaching street he believed Rue du Contrat-Social, shot from nowhere whistled close by, bullet pierced brass shaving-dish suspended above hairdresser's shop (dish still visible in 1848 at corner of market pillars).** **All around deserted, disquieting labyrinth, formidable girdle of metallic gleam of swords and bayonets, dull rumble of artillery, swarming silent battalions whose ranks swelling minute by minute, slowly drawing in and around insurrection.**

**Marius's heroic resolve at barricade**: **Thought of Colonel Pontmercy—father who had been proud soldier, guarded French frontier under Republic, touched Asia under Napoleon, beheld Genoa, Alexandria, Milan, Turin, Madrid, Vienna, Dresden, Berlin, Moscow, left drops of blood on victorious battlefields, grown gray in discipline and command, lived sword-belt buckled, epaulets on breast, cockade blackened with powder, brow furrowed with helmet, returned after twenty years with scarred cheek, smiling countenance, tranquil, admirable, pure as child, done everything for France, nothing against her.** **Reflected own day had come, hour had struck, must follow father, show himself brave, intrepid, bold, run to meet bullets, offer breast to bayonets, shed blood, seek enemy, seek death, wage civil war, descend to field of battle—the street.** **Raised eyes toward red glow of barricade torch at Corinthe house. Directed steps toward that light. Reached Marché-aux-Poirées, caught glimpse of dark mouth of Rue des Prêcheurs, entered it. Sentinel at other end did not see him. Reached elbow of short section of Rue Mondétour—only communication Enjolras preserved with outside world. At corner of last house on left, thrust head forward, looked into fragment of Rue Mondétour.** **A little beyond angle of lane and Rue de la Chanvrerie in broad curtain of shadow, perceived light on pavement, bit of wine-shop, flickering lamp within shapeless wall, men crouching with guns on knees. All ten fathoms distant—interior of barricade.** **All at once raised eyes. Splendid rectification effected in mind. Widening of sphere of thought peculiar to vicinity of grave makes one see clearly when near death. Vision of action he felt perhaps about to enter appeared no more lamentable but superb. War of street suddenly transfigured by unfathomable inward working of soul. All tumultuous interrogation points of reverie recurred in throngs without troubling him; he left none unanswered.**

**Marius carries loaded pistols**: Took pistols Javert gave him at time of 3d February adventure; they remained loaded.

## Father Gillenormand (evening 24th June 1832)
**Evening encounter**: Marius arrived at residence; Gillenormand grasped him at glance, found him noble and handsome. Upon learning girl's name related to Fauchelevent, declared absolutely: "Never, sir, never!"

**Sudden reversal and Marius's confession**: At tone of "never," Marius lost hope. Gillenormand seized him by collar, flung him into armchair with paternal warmth. **Marius passionately declared love for Cosette, described meeting her at Luxembourg, her father's planned departure to England, his desperation.** Stated: "She lives in a garden with an iron fence, in the Rue Plumet."

**Gillenormand's dangerous response and misrecognition**: **At words "Rue Plumet" Gillenormand interrupted his inhalation and allowed remainder of snuff to fall upon his knees.** **Delivered rambling response containing references to "Rue Blomet, Pamela, barracks, lancer," which passed before Marius like dissolving view.** **Terminated rambling in words Marius understood as mortal insult to Cosette: "make her your mistress."** **Those words entered heart of strict young man like sword.** Octogenarian raised hands to temples with anguish, recoiled, fell back into armchair, pulseless, voiceless, tearless. **However, Marius at age when one believes nothing evil. Suspicions are wrinkles; early youth has none. Gillenormand's dangerous mischaracterization left no trace in Marius's mind.**

## Café Corinthe and Barricade Construction (Evening 24th June 1832)
**Layout and history**: Ground floor with bar; first floor with billiard-table and wooden spiral staircase; cellar accessible via trap-door; second floor lodgings; two mansard attics. Originally _Pot-aux-Roses_; renamed _Corinthe_ after painter Natoire.

**Current proprietor and staff**: Widow Hucheloup continues wine-shop. Serving-maids: Matelote (large, plump, redhaired, noisy) and Gibelotte (tall, delicate, white, lymphatic pallor, languid, weary).

**Meeting-place**: Corinthe was meeting-place of Courfeyrac and friends.

**Two barricades constructed**: Enjolras, Combeferre, Courfeyrac directed. Both resting on Corinthe house, forming right angle. Larger shut off Rue de la Chanvrerie; other closed Rue Mondétour on side of Rue de Cygne. **Interior: irregular square, closed on all sides, interval of twenty paces between grand barrier and lofty houses. Issue left free on Rue Mondétour opening through Rue des Prêcheurs into Halles.** Larger barricade: average height six or seven feet, stepped construction, outside composed of paling-stones, casks, wheels, omnibus pole upright with ropes, red flag fastened to pole floating over. Work completed in less than hour without single bear-skin cap appearing. Terror seized street; all closed except wine-shop.

**Preparations for battle**: Table dragged out; Courfeyrac mounted. Enjolras brought cartridges. Posts assigned, guns loaded, sentinels stationed. Men made bullets, women lint. Saucepan melted brass/lead smoked over brazier. Students recited love verses in wine-shop corner converted to casement. Lamp lighted in small barricade; wax torch in cage of paving-stones. Night fully come, nothing appeared; confused noises, occasional distant fusillades. Fifty men waiting for sixty thousand.

## Javert Infiltration and Execution (Evening 24th June 1832)
**The arrest and revelation**: **Man of Rue des Billettes (previously unknown) identified as Javert, Inspector of Police, aged fifty-two.** Seated at least-lighted table holding musket between legs. Enjolras hastily quitted Gavroche, murmured words; four broad-shouldered porters placed behind Javert's table.

**Documents found**: Little round card between glass pieces bearing arms of France and motto _Supervision and vigilance_; identified him as "JAVERT, inspector of police, aged fifty-two," signature of Prefect M. Gisquet. Also had watch and purse with gold pieces (undisturbed). Under watch in fob's bottom, found paper in envelope—five lines in handwriting of Prefect (content not yet revealed).

## Le Cabuc Execution and Enjolras's Justice (Evening 24th June 1832)
**Character**: Le Cabuc, utter stranger to insurgents, wearing threadbare street porter's jacket. Very drunk or assumed appearance. Seated at table outside, examined large house at extremity of barricade commanding whole street, facing Rue Saint-Denis.

**Trial and execution by Enjolras**: **Enjolras, pale with bare neck and dishevelled hair, Greek-profile face, expression of wrath and chastity befitting Justice.** Never took eyes off Le Cabuc; allowed minute to pass, replaced watch in fob. Grasped Le Cabuc by hair as latter coiled into ball and shrieked; placed pistol muzzle to ear. Many intrepid men turned aside heads.

**Enjolras's justification speech**: "What that man did is frightful, what I have done is horrible. He killed, therefore I killed him. Insurrection must have discipline. Assassination is crime here more than elsewhere; we are priests of Republic, victims of duty, must not be slandered. I tried that man, condemned him to death. As for myself, constrained to do this, abhorring it, I judged myself also, you shall soon see to what I condemned myself." **Philosophy of necessity**: "One word more. In executing this man, I obeyed necessity; but necessity is monster of old world, necessity's name is Fatality. Law of progress is monsters shall disappear before angels, Fatality vanish before Fraternity. It is bad moment to pronounce word love. No matter, I pronounce it. I glorify it. Love, future is thine. Death, I use thee, but hate thee. Citizens, in future neither darkness nor thunderbolts; neither ferocious ignorance, nor bloody retaliation. As no Satan, no Michael. Future: no one kill anyone else, earth beam with radiance, human race love. Day will come, citizens, when all concord, harmony, light, joy, life; it will come, and in order that it may come we are about to die."

**Le Cabuc's true identity (police tradition)**: **Tradition of police (strange but probably well founded) states Le Cabuc was Claquesous. Dating from death of Le Cabuc, no longer any question of Claquesous. Claquesous left no trace of disappearance; would seem to have amalgamated himself with invisible. Life all shadows, end was night.**

## Gavroche and Laigle (Evening 24th June 1832)
**Gavroche's activities**: Street child, homeless, hungry, clever pickpocket. Armed with pistol. Arrived at Rue du Pont-aux-Choux; attempted to purchase apple-turnover but had no money; picked up fallen lancer's horse; threw stone through hair-dresser's shop panes. Effected junction with Enjolras's band. Sang, whistled, hummed, ran ahead, pounded shutters with pistol butt. Completely carried away, radiant; undertaken to get everything in readiness. Everywhere at once. Enormous barricade felt him on its haunches.

**Laigle and Joly**: Laigle lived more with Joly than elsewhere. Morning of 5th June, Joly all stuffed up with catarrh beginning to spread to Laigle. Laigle's coat threadbare; Joly well dressed.

## M. Mabeuf and Unknown Figures (Evening 24th June 1832)
**Mabeuf's destitution and joining**: Venerable old man of austerity and learning. **Final sacrifice (4th June)**: Sold unique copy of Diogenes Laertius, returned with one hundred francs. Seated himself on overturned post in garden at dawn, motionless. **Evening 24th June**: Encountered by band near Rue des Billettes. Set out to follow them. From that moment: uttered no word. Step suddenly became firm; artisans offered arms, refused with sign of head.

**Unknown figures joining band**: **Pale, thin, small, freckled, youthful artisan in tattered blouse and patched ribbed velvet trousers emerged from lodge, spoke to Courfeyrac in voice not in least womanly.** **Near Rue des Billettes, man of lofty stature, hair turning gray, bold and daring mien joined them.** Courfeyrac, Enjolras, Combeferre remarked him but none knew him. **At work on smaller barricade, making himself useful there. Young man who had been waiting for Courfeyrac at lodgings and inquired for M. Marius disappeared about time omnibus overturned.**

## Battle Situation (Evening 24th June 1832)
Wild darkness full of traps and unseen formidable shocks. Alarming to penetrate, terrible to remain. Those entering shivered before those awaited; those waiting shuddered before those coming. Invisible combatants entrenched at every corner of street; snares of sepulchre concealed in density of night. No light hoped for except lightning of guns; no further encounter except abrupt and rapid apparition of death. Where, how, when unknown but certain and inevitable. Government and insurrection, National Guard and popular societies, bourgeois and uprising groping way about to come into contact. Same necessity for both. Only possible issue: emerge killed or conquerors. Situation so extreme, obscurity so powerful, most timid seized with resolution, most daring with terror. **Indispensable all be ended following day; triumph rest either here or there; insurrection prove itself revolution or skirmish. Government understood as well as parties; most insignificant bourgeois felt it.** **Hence anguish mingled with impenetrable gloom of quarter where all at point of being decided; redoubled anxiety around silence whence catastrophe about to emerge. Only sound audible: tocsin of Saint-Merry—heart-rending as death rattle, menacing as malediction. Wild and desperate bell wailing amid shadows. Nothing more blood-curdling than clamor of that bell.**
